title: I've build a trading bot
author: Conscious-Driver-146
selftext:
I've build a trading bot and backtested it over 16 years of real cme data of NAS, ES, YM & Russell. I've made a bunch of out of sample backtests, monte carlo analysis, walk forward analysis & plateau. 

The strategy still performed very nice on all those tests. I even calculated the avg. spread/splippage into the strategy. 

Did I really find a profitable strategy? Or am I just lucky? 

As you can see the strat wasn't profitable from 2010 - 2015, but from 2016 - 2026 roughly 100R every year which is nuts. 

I'm currently running a shadow phase where I let the strategy run on real live data.

https://i.redd.it/4f643qdix82i1.png

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: six flat years and then ten great ones usually means the rules got shaped on the great ones, even when every single test after that was run honestly. what did you fit the parameters on, the whole 16 years or only the stretch after 2016?

replies.author: Conscious-Driver-146
replies.body: Parameters were 2023-2026, the rest is out of sample

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: ah, that flips it, fitting on the last three years and testing backwards is more honest than I assumed. the six flat years still bug me though: it only worked out of sample from 2016 on, so it may be catching a regime that started then, and 2023-26 sits in the same one.

replies.author: Few-Instruction-2087
replies.body: I believe the index futures fundamentally changed in behaviour after the late 2010s, the regime has never reverted to the early 2010s since,. especially after the COVID boom.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: could be, but 'it changed after covid' is also exactly how an overfit looks the day it stops working. I'd want the bot to name what changed, overnight gaps or the volatility level, and show it holding on years it never saw before I'd trust the regime story.

replies.author: Few-Instruction-2087
replies.body: Volume and volatility, much larger ATR, significant jumps in retail participation etc. These factors are documented and not just my personal observations. Of course, if somehow volume dies off and participation in these futures markets significantly reduces then the regime will naturally shift again. I have a couple strats that work well on the current regime and have been tested on a few years of unseen data 23-26, but if we go back to market conditions from the early 2010s these would fail as they rely on the large NQ ranges and it's general high volatility.

comments.author: AoideusWasBanned
comments.body: Did you check it per instrument? If NAS carries most of the 2016+ years and the other three are flat, it might be riding the tech trend more than an edge.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Good that you're running a shadow phase, because that's the test that counts. One thing in your chart to think about is that the old period, labelled out of sample, lost money, and the profitable era only starts after it. If the 2015 start date was picked after seeing the curve, then the good stretch isn't really out of sample. I'd ask whether anything in the rules explains why the market changed then, apart from the results. Also set the pass or fail line for the shadow phase now, before it ends, so the answer is clear. If you want another way to check, Cymetica's Backtest Labs holds out the last part of the history, which gives you a test you can't tune around.

replies.author: Conscious-Driver-146
replies.body:
Fair points, appreciate it. On the 2015 cut: it actually wasn't picked after seeing the curve. The strategy was built on 2021-2026 only, then I bought 2015-2021 data and ran 2015-2020 as a true OOS — it passed before the 2010-2015 data even existed on my machine. The 2015 boundary came from data availability, not from the equity curve. When I later bought 2010-2015 as a second OOS, the thresholds and the interpretation were pre-registered in writing before I looked at the data.

To your question whether anything besides the results explains the regime change: partially, yes. Decomposing the 2010-2015 losses by session shows the NY core was actually slightly positive (+54R) even back then — the entire loss came from the London window (-151R), where the edge simply didn't exist before \~2019. Same picture under three different cost models. So it's a structural finding, not just "the curve looks bad before 2015". The deeper why (microstructure/HFT era) is plausible but I can't prove it, and there are data caveats pre-2015 (CME system-priced trades), so I treat it as regime-dependent and size expectations off the post-2015 era plus the shadow phase — not off the full 16 years.

Fully agree on pre-registering the shadow pass/fail line — doing that now: minimum sample (\~2-3 months / 60-80 trades), signal parity vs. backtest, limit fill rate vs. the backtest's touch assumption, and cumulative R staying above the Monte Carlo P5 band. London gets monitored separately with its own kill criterion.

Btw, couldn't find anything called Cymetica Backtest Labs anywhere — got a link? Either way, a holdout can't help me retroactively since I've already seen the full history; the only data I can't tune around is forward data, which is what the shadow phase is for.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Fair enough, that answers my question well. A boundary set by data availability is a clean reason, and the pre-registered thresholds and the separate London kill criterion are good. You're also right that a holdout can't help after you've seen the full history. On the link, Backtest Labs is a tool inside Cymetica's platform, and I work at Cymetica, so take that mention as biased. Searching Cymetica should find it. For your case, the shadow phase with the line you set is the better test.
